title: Social Engineering: Email Spoofing
summary: Email Spoofing is the header-manipulation form of Social Engineering, in which the adversary falsifies sender fields so that mail appears to originate from a domain the sender does not control. Unlike general impersonation, which may rely on a lookalike address or a compromised mailbox, spoofing forges the envelope and From values themselves, and it succeeds wherever domain authentication is missing or unenforced. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) authorises sending servers, DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) signs messages, and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) states how failures should be handled; a published but unenforced policy instructs receivers to take no action, so failed mail still lands in the inbox. Detection depends on reading Authentication-Results and Received headers, comparing the aligned domain against the visible From address, and watching for internal-looking mail that entered from an external source or from an unauthenticated device on the local network.

beginner.definition: Email spoofing means an attacker fakes the sender of an email. The message can be made to look like it came from your bank or your manager. The attacker only changes the address shown in the sender fields. It is different from copying a name, because here the sender address itself is false.
beginner.whyItMatters: We are told to check the sender address, and a spoofed address appears correct. Your domain may have no mail authentication rule at all. The rule may only report problems and take no action, so the fake message still arrives. Attackers use this for payment fraud, password requests, and dangerous attachments. Setting the rules correctly is one of the cheapest defences you can add.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses a domain to pretend to be, such as a bank or partner.
They send email from their own server but write the trusted address in the header fields.
If the receiver has no checks, the message is delivered and looks genuine.
SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks exist to catch this, but only if the domain owner sets them up.
A policy that says take no action lets failed mail reach the inbox anyway.
The attacker may also use a local device, such as a printer, to send unauthenticated mail.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat where post is left on a hallway table. Anyone can write a friend's name on a blank envelope, drop it on the table, and walk away. The handwriting looks new, but the name is familiar, so the flatmate opens it without a thought. The envelope was never checked, and the sender was invented.
takeaways: Check the mail authentication headers, not only the sender name shown in your client.
Publish an enforcing mail policy for your own domains so failures are blocked.
Treat internal-looking mail that came from outside as suspicious.

objectives: Explain how email spoofing differs from the parent technique Social Engineering.
Describe what SPF, DKIM, and DMARC each verify, and how they work together.
Explain why a non-enforcing mail policy allows forged mail to be delivered.
Identify the header fields an analyst reads to confirm a spoofed sender.
Describe how unauthenticated internal sending devices can be abused to fake internal mail.
